title: A cache expiry rewritten as a stored deadline, proved on every nanosecond and the sentinel
summary: A cache's expire-after-write test is "has the time to live elapsed since the write". A developer rewrites it as "is now past the deadline", computing the deadline once at write time so that an eviction wheel can index entries by it, and guards the one addition that can overflow. The module's properties file says an entry expires exactly when its time to live has elapsed, and an entry that lives forever never does. The prover shows the rewrite satisfies it on all 2^192 inputs, including the `Long.MAX_VALUE` sentinel and the deadlines the addition cannot represent.

change.description: Compute `expiresAtNanos = writtenAtNanos + ttlNanos` and compare the clock with it, keeping the `FOREVER` check, and treating a deadline the addition wraps as one the clock will never reach. The tests for expiring on time and for `FOREVER` pass.

risk: None, and that is the point. The rewrite is the one that goes wrong in cache libraries: a time to live near `Long.MAX_VALUE`, which is what "a very long time" is spelled as in configuration, overflows the addition, the deadline wraps to a negative number, and every entry is expired at birth, which turns a cache into a slower way of calling the backend, with no error anywhere. The developer knew this and added the guard; the question for the reviewer is whether the guard, the sentinel and the comparison agree with the old rule at every edge, and the edges are at 2^63, where no test suite goes by accident.
explanation: The property reads: for every write time, every positive time to live and every clock reading not before the write, the method returns true exactly when the time to live is not `FOREVER` and the elapsed time has reached it. The elapsed-time form on the right-hand side is the old rule itself, so the property is a regression statement as well as a specification. JBMC proves the patched method satisfies it over the whole domain, three 64-bit numbers, in a few seconds. A sampling test could not say this: the inputs that matter are the ones within a few units of `Long.MAX_VALUE`, which is where the guard decides.
resolution: Merge. The property stays in the file, so a later change that drops the guard, or the sentinel, is refuted with the input that breaks it.
provenance: Constructed from the deadline form of expire-after-write in Caffeine, whose `Long.MAX_VALUE` handling exists because of the overflow this rewrite guards against.

references.title: Spring Framework, Cache Abstraction with Caffeine
